newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Boral gas unit seen expanding after float.
newsitem.headline: Boral gas unit seen expanding after float.

text.p: Boral Ltd's float of its gas distribution businesses would set up the new company to bid for gas and electricity distribution assets in Victoria and New South Wales, analysts said on Monday.

Ann Diamant, oil and gas analyst with brokerage firm Hartley Poynton, told Reuters that Envestra Ltd was likely to bid for some of Victoria's Gas and Fuel Corp assets when it was privatised, and would be interested in any New South Wales (NSW) electricity assets to be sold.

"I think the reason they are doing this is because they want to be proactive in terms of what is going to be happening in the energy industry and it is not appropriate for Boral to be highly geared whereas for a distribution network (it is)," Diamant said.
Analyst John Hirjee from First Pacific Stockbroking said there would be no shortage of opportunities but continuing overseas interest would ensure that the assets would not be cheap.

The NSW government has estimated that its electricity assets were worth up to A$26 billion while the Victorian assets have a value of up to A$5 billion, with both states to conduct sales on a piecemeal basis.

"AGL is in a similar position, both will have the problem that they will be damned if they pay too much and they will be damned if they do not get it, so it really is going to be competitive," Hirjee said.

"There will have to be some serious thinking about where companies want to be - do they want to be in distribution, transmission or upstream - and I think Boral is hedging its bets a little (with this float)," he said, adding that First Pacific had valued the distribution business at A$740-$765 million.

Boral, a company that is mainly involved in the building products sector, said at a news conference on Monday morning that it expected to raise more than A$850 million through the float of its gas distribution networks in South Australia, Queensland and Northern Territory. It would retain an active 19.9 percent stake in Envestra Ltd.

Standard and Poor's said the move was "strategically neutral" for Boral as the division accounted for only a small part of overall revenue of A$4.7 billion. Still, the division was in a low-risk business and its cash flow was relatively stable, the ratings agency said in its affirmation of Boral's ratings.

Boral Energy, which lumps the gas operations with oil and gas exploration/production, had 1995/96 sales of A$784 million and was the largest divisional profit contributor with earnings of A$135 million.
Under the float structure, 60 percent of the stock would be publicly offered to Boral shareholders, 20 percent to institutions, and 19.9 percent would be kept by Boral.

Hirjee said parts of Boral's strategy were not yet clear, namely why it chose a float ahead other mechanisms and why it only wanted a 20 percent stake in Envestra if it wanted to participate in further utility busineses.
"If the concept is a good one, why float it off and why dilute your exposure and then buy some more," he said.
"I would have thought they would have floated the upstream (operations) and kept the distribution businesses because that gives you the secure revenue base," he said.
Another analyst, who did not want to be named, said he was suprised by how much Boral was aiming to raise and expected interest to come chiefly from overseas utilities groups.
"You have got to sit back and say why should the shareholders who already own the assets have to pay close to top dollar to buy the distribution assets that are there," he said.
